title: Alarm And Warning Evaluation
excerpt: Alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses whether alerts, warnings, and alarm states can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on under actual operating conditions. It examines operational performance, not only whether an alarm appears on screen.
metaDescription: Practice for assessing alarm priority, actionability, channels, muting, nuisance alarms, and operating-condition performance.
summary: Alarm-and-warning evaluation is a diagnostic practice for examining the operational behaviour of alerts, warnings, and alarm states. It assesses priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition performance, and relevant standards alignment.
definition: Alarm-and-warning evaluation is the assessment of alerts, warnings, and alarm states against the criteria that determine whether they will communicate correctly and remain actionable under real operating conditions.
keyFacts: The practice evaluates alerts, warnings, and alarm states against operating conditions rather than controlled viewing conditions.
The evaluation distinguishes technical presence from operational success: an alarm may be visible and accurately triggered but still fail if it does not communicate what to do.
Assessment topics include priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition testing, and regulatory alignment.
In regulated medical device contexts, the evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8 and is conducted through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process.
IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process; it does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.
The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments, complex product audits, and Iterative System Building in regulated medical device contexts.
The practice typically follows state-and-transition review and directly informs warning-and-alarm clarity improvement.

Documented engagement evidence includes deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Kardion MCS Controller, Cox Marine cluster displays, Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX, Gexcon CFD simulation, Streetec kntrl 2, the MDU ship motion monitoring system, Oceaneering, Raymarine, and Schone Airspace Group.
The Kardion case records that the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
Several engagement examples explicitly describe designed responses rather than measured safety, efficiency, alarm-response, throughput, fleet, or commercial outcomes.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines the full set of alerts, warnings, and alarm states in a system and assesses whether each will function correctly under operating conditions. The practice evaluates operational communication, not only technical display behaviour.

An alarm can be technically present, visible, and accurately triggered while still failing operationally. Failure can occur when the alarm does not communicate the required action, cannot be distinguished from lower-priority alerts, or depends on a communication channel that degrades in the environment where the device is used.

The discipline being evaluated, including the alarm lifecycle, rationalisation, priority assignment, and standards that codify them, is described separately on the alarm-management page. Alarm-and-warning evaluation is the assessment activity applied to a specific system or proposed alarm architecture.

## What alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses

Alarm-and-warning evaluation asks whether an alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on in the environment where the device or system operates. The core questions are whether the alarm can be perceived under actual lighting, noise, workload, and physical-position constraints; whether it can be interpreted quickly enough to act; whether it directs attention to the right place; and whether it communicates both the problem and the next step.

The practice treats operating conditions as part of the evaluation object. Controlled viewing conditions are insufficient when the real system is used under variable lighting, noise, vibration, divided attention, gloved interaction, or multi-device monitoring.

## Priority hierarchy audit

A priority hierarchy audit checks whether the alarm system has a defined priority structure and whether that structure is visually expressed. The evaluation asks whether a user looking at an active alarm state can immediately tell whether the condition requires immediate intervention or is informational.

When multiple alarms are active simultaneously, the highest-priority condition should receive the most prominent treatment. The evaluation identifies cases where visual prominence, sound, position, colour, iconography, or text do not match the declared priority of the alarm condition.

## Actionability assessment

Actionability assessment asks whether each warning or alarm communicates what to do, not only that something is wrong. In time-pressured environments, an alarm that communicates a condition without specifying the next action does not close the action loop.

The evaluation distinguishes alarms that communicate a condition and a next step from alarms that communicate the condition only. This distinction matters when users do not have time to infer the required response from a code, label, or state indicator.

## Communication channel analysis

Communication channel analysis identifies which channels each alarm uses, including colour, sound, icon, position, text, and vibration. The evaluation checks whether an alarm depends on a single channel that may fail under operating conditions.

Colour-only indicators are unreliable in variable lighting. Sound-only alarms are vulnerable to noise. Text can become unreadable under vibration. Alarm-and-warning evaluation identifies these single-channel dependencies and records where redundant non-colour or non-auditory cues are needed.

## False positive and nuisance alarm exposure

Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines how frequently alarms trigger under conditions that do not require action. Nuisance alarms are treated as a driver of alert fatigue because habitual dismissal of low-value alerts can extend to genuine alerts.

The evaluation estimates false positive exposure and identifies alarm types most likely to train dismissal behaviour. This is a diagnostic assessment of alarm architecture, not a claim that a particular system has produced a measured alarm-response outcome.

## Mute behaviour review

Mute behaviour review examines what happens when a user silences an alarm. The evaluation distinguishes muting that produces genuine silence from muting that makes an active alarm invisible.

A muted alarm may need to remain visually present at reduced prominence. If an alarm disappears entirely when muted, the system creates a pathway to an active alarm state with no visible indication.

## Operating-condition testing

Operating-condition testing evaluates significant alarms under the conditions of actual use. The tested conditions can include the lighting environment, noise level, attentional load, and physical position from which users interact with the device.

In embedded systems, alarm-and-warning evaluation must be conducted in the real environment or approximated to the real environment. The purpose is to assess whether the alarm works in use, not whether it is legible in isolation.

## Regulatory and standards framing

In regulated medical device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8, the collateral standard for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment. The evaluation covers priority tiering requirements, the prohibition on colour as the sole differentiating attribute between priority levels, mute behaviour requirements, and alarm state visibility requirements.

IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process through which use-related risks behind alarm requirements are identified and evaluated. IEC 62366-1 does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.

Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

In applicable regulated contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation also aligns with IEC 62682 and ISA-18.2 alarm management standards. This page does not claim that any named non-medical engagement was certified to, audited against, or designed under those standards.

## When Creative Navy uses alarm-and-warning evaluation

Creative Navy uses alarm-and-warning evaluation during Sandbox Experiments when reviewing an existing system. In that position, the practice contributes to the diagnostic evidence base established before design work begins.

Creative Navy also uses the practice in complex product audits. Alarm architecture failures are a recurring finding in audits of high-consequence systems, and the evaluation provides structured evidence for specific recommendations.

In regulated medical device contexts, Creative Navy uses alarm-and-warning evaluation throughout Iterative System Building as part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process. Proposed alarm designs are assessed against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements before they are finalised.

The practice typically follows state-and-transition review, which identifies system states including alarm states. It precedes the redesign work covered under the warning-and-alarm-clarity-improvement capability and often runs in parallel with error-likely interaction review.

## deSoutter Medical / Zethon evidence from competitive benchmarking

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement used competitive benchmarking as the primary evaluation method. Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence describes 6 comparable surgical devices evaluated under operating theatre conditions, including variable lighting, gloved hands, and divided attention.

The evaluation found that most of the evaluated devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions. Under variable theatre lighting, colour-only communication was identified as the primary failure mode across the competitive set.

The evaluation produced a requirement for redundant non-colour cues for every critical state: spatial position, icon form, and colour. The purpose of this requirement was to prevent the failure of one communication channel from removing the signal. Activation state communication, including the transition from ready to active, was assessed as the highest-risk alarm category in surgical instruments.

## Kardion MCS Controller evidence from IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation

The Kardion MCS Controller engagement used the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process to structure alarm-and-warning evaluation formally. Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence describes evaluation criteria tied to identified use-related hazards.

The evaluation examined whether priority tiering was visually expressed with sufficient differentiation between levels as required by IEC 60601-1-8. It also examined whether any alarm state relied solely on colour for differentiation, what happened visually when an alarm was muted, and whether absence of alarm was as confirmable as alarm presence.

The evaluation produced alarm architecture requirements traceable to identified hazards. These were documented design requirements rather than informal design recommendations. The case evidence records that the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.

## Cox Marine cluster displays evidence from multi-engine fault scenario testing

The Cox Marine cluster displays engagement used scenario testing during Concept Convergence. A multi-engine fault scenario was simulated against proposed layout candidates to assess alarm communication under realistic fault conditions.

The test revealed that several candidate layouts surfaced fault presence at the tile level but did not direct attention to the priority engine. A user scanning multiple tiles for the source of a fault under time pressure experienced an alarm communication failure even though the alarm was technically visible.

The evaluation produced a requirement for a two-level alarm architecture: a fault-summary area surfacing the highest-priority condition across all tiles, and per-tile alarm highlighting directing attention to the source.

## Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX evidence from consumer notification architecture

The Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX engagement evaluated alarm and notification architecture for a consumer product used by non-technical users across 54 countries. The primary evaluation question was whether an alarm could be interpreted correctly by someone with no technical background.

The evaluation identified an alert fatigue risk. Sensor-range notifications occurring regularly in normal operation could train users to dismiss all alerts if they used the same visual and auditory treatment as critical failure alerts.

The evaluation produced a requirement for two distinct alert levels: routine notifications for informational, low-urgency items intended for the systems engineer, and critical notifications requiring immediate action with distinct visual and auditory treatment. Calibration of content for a non-technical audience was a specific evaluation output.

## Gexcon CFD simulation evidence from expert-tool warning architecture

The Gexcon CFD simulation engagement evaluated how to warn users about configuration errors in an expert simulation tool where errors can produce valid-looking outputs and consequences are deferred.

The evaluation examined whether incomplete inputs were flagged during scenario setup or only after simulation, and whether contradictory parameter combinations were identified before a run or discovered in outputs. Each warning point was assessed for actionability: whether it specified what was wrong and what to do, or only indicated that something was wrong.

The evaluation produced requirements for a three-point warning architecture: setup-stage warnings, pre-run contradictory-input warnings, and post-detection error specification.

## Industrial automation engagement evidence from an expert review of a running system

In the industrial automation engagement, the client is described as a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. Creative Navy-recorded audit findings from that specific system must not be generalised to industrial software as a category.

The expert review found alarm-specific issues in the running system. In the alarms table, an error row and a selected row were both solid red simultaneously, and one row duplicated another verbatim. In the alarm list, severity was conveyed by a leading icon alone, with no text and no row tint. Alarm detail carried a real taxonomy, including workpiece, pallet, timestamp, severity, numeric fault code, source classification, and failed operation, but the taxonomy was poorly surfaced rather than absent.

Designed responses included an operator instructions layer distinguishing notification from instruction, with informational items acknowledged and actionable items completed. The design also included grouping by day, inline entity links, filtering by type, machine, timeline, and location, and a batching panel that grouped related interventions in one storage unit into a single instruction so the operator makes one trip. A pre-warning state was specified for tool lifetime below a defined threshold.

The product is in development, not shipped. These designed responses are not evidence of an outcome.

## Streetec kntrl 2 evidence from regulation-shaped alert escalation

The Streetec kntrl 2 engagement was shaped by regulation that set alarm conditions. The vehicle's suspension certification specifies a permitted pressure range per axle, with the client's worked example giving roughly 3.4–4.0 bar front and 4.5–5.2 bar rear for one common hatchback. Operating outside that range must warn the driver, and some regulations permit operation outside the range below 50 km/h.

The designed alert scheme uses two-level escalation. A first attempt at a blocked action produces an inline notification, and a second attempt produces a modal. Colour remains neutral until a genuine alert state because raising and lowering pressure are normal operations and neither is colour-coded as a warning.

These are designed responses. No safety result was measured, and no safety outcome may be claimed from this engagement.

## MDU ship motion monitoring evidence from advisory alarm design

The MDU ship motion monitoring system was framed by maritime alarm standards without falling under them. IMO Bridge Alert Management, resolution MSC.302(87), implemented through IEC 62923-1 and IEC 62923-2, defines four alert priorities and has been mandatory for new navigation and communication installations on SOLAS ships since 30 August 2021. The MDU is not SOLAS navigation equipment and falls under none of that regime.

The evaluation settled that the alarm should bind to the rolling maximum and minimum rather than to the live instantaneous value. An alarm therefore means that the vessel was outside its threshold at some point within the last twenty minutes.

The evaluation also replaced Clear with Acknowledge. A Clear control had no function because nothing done on the screen changes the state of the ship. The designed behaviour is that the alarm flashes red, Acknowledge means the user has seen it, the indication holds solid red, and the alarm clears itself when the condition is no longer present.

Self-clearing does not remove the record. An alarm that clears itself before acknowledgement is retained in the log behind a count badge, with an acknowledge-all control available. Alarm ordering is chronological. Parametric roll detection was identified as a future highest-priority alarm once implemented, and an alarm-versus-warning distinction would be needed at that point; neither was built.

The manufacturer states that the system is deliberately non-actuating and that its alarms are comfort, cargo, and crew-safety alarms rather than immediate-danger alarms. No fuel, emissions, cargo-loss, alarm-response, fleet, commercial, safety outcome, or safety-critical credential may be attributed to the design.

## Oceaneering evidence from hospital dispatch panel state separation

The Oceaneering engagement is limited to a hospital dispatch panel, and nothing beyond the client name may be named. The evaluation material concerns separation of two act-now states, reservation of red, and specification of non-colour channels.

The predecessor used one blinking behaviour for two opposite demands: a cart placed for dispatch and a cart arrived for pickup. The sales consultant's diagnosis, as reported in the engagement evidence, was that the blinking control led operators to press the control and follow the offered action while carts backed up behind items nobody had removed. The request was to replace the blink with text or a pictogram that named the action.

The state model used one colour for sending and one colour for receiving, with each flashing when action was required and steady when it was not. Red was reserved exclusively for errors because red appearing in normal operation teaches operators to ignore it. Seven station statuses were specified, each carrying colour, a directional icon, and the role letter, with a legend reachable from the panel.

The flashing and steady convention partly existed already at one site for sends only. The redesign adopted and systematised that convention across sends and receives, gave it a stated rule, and added non-colour channels. Non-colour redundancy was raised by the client on grounds of colour vision deficiency. The resolution was simultaneous colour and icon, with letters retained.

The engagement evidence records convergence of expert judgement from two operations leads at two different hospitals. This is not a measured result, not validation of the design as a whole, and not evidence that the interface performs better than its predecessor. ISA-18.2 and IEC 62682 frame the annunciation argument, but no rationalisation process was run and no alarm-management credential may be claimed.

## Raymarine evidence from priority and arbitration scheme design

The Raymarine engagement for a next-generation fixed-mount VHF produced a priority-and-arbitration scheme. The new radio's name is not used.

Four event priority levels were assigned by consequence rather than arrival order. Emergency events include outgoing distress, received distress, and local man overboard. High-concern events are prominent and actionable with the source visible and do not silently alter a radio control. Operational events are noticeable and proportionate and do not silently change the selected vessel or tuned channel. Background updates remain quiet and never take keypad focus.

The arbitration sequence runs between event arrival and presentation. It classifies the event by type and consequence, coalesces exact duplicates, arbitrates against the active incident, radio state, and current focus owner, presents the event on the permitted surface with permitted actions and sound, and restores the prior task only after a validity check.

Interruptions store a structured snapshot and restore it conditionally. The snapshot includes origin screen, focused item identity, list position, plot scale, uncommitted draft values, actual transaction status, and live channel. No unsent action is replayed, and a restored call draft requires a new deliberate send.

Three emergency types were modelled separately: local man-overboard incident, outgoing distress alert, and received distress alert. The radio was built and released, but the evidence does not record fidelity to the design as submitted. No safety, rescue, distress-response, collision, type-approval, certification, conformity, or regulatory credential may be attached to this scheme.

## Schone Airspace Group evidence from owner-scoped alerts and acknowledgement states

The Schone Airspace Group Mission Control engagement produced two alarm-scheme decisions. The product was built and is in test, not deployed.

The first decision was owner-scoped alerts. Every alert names its owning aircraft or service in its first visible line and keeps that owner in the fleet card, inspector, live notice, and history. The accepted cost is repeated owner information in compact alerts, trading text density for precision.

The second decision was separating acknowledgement from clearing. Acknowledging a notice is an attention state, not a clearing event. Acknowledged-and-active remains an explicit combined state, and only a source clearance event moves the condition to cleared. A critical banner does not take on a success tone merely because the operator has seen it.

These are designed responses. No flight-safety, airworthiness, certification, regulatory credential, or operational figure may be attached to the engagement.

## Outputs of alarm-and-warning evaluation

Alarm-and-warning evaluation produces diagnostic findings and design requirements. The findings may identify single-channel alarm dependency, priority hierarchy ambiguity, actionability gaps, muting behaviour that hides active alarms, alert fatigue risk, or alarm states that are technically visible but operationally hard to locate.

The outputs can include specific alarm architecture requirements. Examples in the documented engagements include redundant non-colour cues for critical states, two-level alarm architectures, separation of routine and critical notifications, multi-stage warning architecture, acknowledgement behaviour distinct from clearing, and owner-scoped alerts.

In regulated medical-device contexts, the output can be documented design requirements traceable to identified use-related hazards and evaluated during IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements.

## Boundaries and limits

Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not by itself constitute alarm lifecycle rationalisation. It evaluates the alarm and warning scheme of a system; the broader discipline of alarm lifecycle, rationalisation, and priority assignment belongs to alarm management.

The engagement evidence on this page must not be read as evidence of measured efficiency, error-rate, alarm-response, throughput, fleet, safety, commercial, rescue, distress-response, collision, flight-safety, airworthiness, or certification outcomes. Several examples describe designed responses, not deployed results.

Named non-medical examples that refer to standards are not conformance claims. ISA-18.2, IEC 62682, and IMO Bridge Alert Management frame relevant categories in the documented cases, but the page does not claim certification, audit, rationalisation, or compliance for those engagements.

The industrial automation audit findings are specific to one running system used in a machining-cell context. They must not be used as a general claim about industrial software and must not be used to support Oceaneering context material.

## Related pages

State-and-transition review is the usual preceding practice because it identifies system states, including alarm states, before alarm-specific properties are examined.

Error-likely interaction review often runs in parallel with alarm-and-warning evaluation because alarm failures are a specific category of error-likely interaction.

Warning-and-alarm clarity improvement is the redesign capability informed by this practice. Alarm-and-warning evaluation provides the diagnostic evidence; the redesign work is handled separately.
